beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: One thousand seven hundred ten bricks. Each column must be forty-five bricks tall. How many columns can we build?

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: I don't know my forty-five times table. Where do I start?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Start with something easy. Ten columns of forty-five use four hundred fifty bricks.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Another ten. And another ten. Thirty columns use three lots of four hundred fifty: one thousand three hundred fifty bricks.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Could we build forty columns?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Forty would need one thousand eight hundred bricks. That's more than we have. Thirty is the largest multiple of ten that fits.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Record thirty as a three in the tens place. Subtract the bricks we used. Three hundred sixty are left.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Forty-five times eight is three hundred sixty. Move those last eight columns into the wall.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Eight goes in the ones place. Subtract three hundred sixty. Nothing left.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: So the three means thirty columns, and the eight means eight columns. Thirty-eight altogether.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: The counts of groups we take are called partial quotients. Here they are thirty and eight.

do.meaning: Counts of groups taken in chunks.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: This wall is also an area model. Its height is forty-five. Each width counts columns; each area counts bricks.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Add the widths for the quotient. Add the areas to check the total. Forty-five times thirty-eight is one thousand seven hundred ten.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Try five hundred ninety-four divided by eighteen. Which first chunk is the largest multiple of ten that fits?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Ten eighteens is one hundred eighty. Thirty is three times that: five hundred forty. It fits.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: But forty needs seven hundred twenty. Too many. So choose thirty.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A smaller chunk can work, but needs more steps. When asked for the largest tens chunk, check that the next ten is too big.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Subtract five hundred forty. Fifty-four remain, enough for three more columns. Thirty plus three is thirty-three.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Divide four thousand three hundred five by twenty-one. Estimate with easy numbers: four thousand divided by twenty is two hundred.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Two hundred columns use four thousand two hundred bricks. Write two in the hundreds place. That leaves one hundred five.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Can we take ten more columns?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Ten would need two hundred ten bricks. We have only one hundred five. No tens fit. Write zero in the tens place.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Five columns use the last one hundred five. Write five in the ones place.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Two hundreds, zero tens, five ones. Two hundred five. Without the zero, twenty-five would be much too small.

do.text: The zero holds the tens place.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Check: twenty-one times two hundred five is four thousand three hundred five. Write zero in any place with no groups, including the ones place.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Four hundred thirty-five chairs, twelve in each row. How many full rows, and how many chairs left over?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Thirty rows use three hundred sixty chairs. Seventy-five are left.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Six more rows use seventy-two chairs. Each dot is one chair.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Three chairs remain. Try to fill the next row.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: We need twelve. Three cannot fill another row.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: So there are thirty-six full rows, with a remainder of three. Remainder means what's left after making every full group possible.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: The remainder must be less than the group size. Otherwise another full row would fit. Check by multiplying, then adding the leftover.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Is this equation true? Multiply one hundred thirty-eight by thirty-three.

do.text: Multiply back to test an equation

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Split the answer into hundreds, tens, and ones. One hundred groups. Thirty groups. Eight groups.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Add the products. Three thousand three hundred plus nine hundred ninety plus two hundred sixty-four equals four thousand five hundred fifty-four. It matches. True.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: What if the equation said one hundred thirty-nine instead?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: That's one extra group of thirty-three. Add thirty-three: four thousand five hundred eighty-seven. The total does not match. False.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Test every equation separately. For a list, select all the true equations requested. For a true-or-false pair, choose one correct statement for each equation.

do.text: For each pair: choose true or false.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Our finished wall: forty-five bricks tall, thirty-eight columns long. The two chunks account for every brick.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Take tens of groups, then ones. For larger answers, start with hundreds. The chunks add up to the answer. Multiply to check.
